summary:
Silent Explorers is an interactive, space-themed digital storybook created to make learning about space exploration more fun and interesting. It takes users on a journey through the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, sharing the stories of robotic explorers and space missions that have travelled far beyond Earth. Instead of simply presenting facts, the project uses storytelling and interactive features to let users explore these missions and discover the incredible journeys of the machines behind them.

The main idea behind this project is to make space science easier to connect with and more enjoyable to explore. Many robotic missions have made remarkable contributions to our understanding of the universe, yet their stories often go unnoticed. Through Silent Explorers, we hope to bring these stories to life, spark curiosity about space, and help people appreciate the silent explorers that continue to uncover the mysteries of our universe.
details: "Letters from the Silent Explorers" is an interactive web experience for kids aged 8-12. Players explore a starry map of the Moon, Mars and deep space, where six glowing markers represent the Apollo 11 descent stage, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Opportunity, Ingenuity and Voyager 1. Each marker opens a card with the machine's first-person "letter" explaining what it is, why it was sent, what it discovered and its status today. Each card also includes a short interactive moment that shows how the machine worked, such as bouncing a laser off the Moon, driving a rover with signal delay, watching a dust storm drain solar power, lifting off a helicopter, or sending a message to Voyager. Every stop links the hardware's engineering to the science it made possible and includes a real mission number from NASA sources. A "Which explorer are you?" quiz ends the experience. Most young space fans only hear about active missions. Our project turns dense mission history into stories that build a personal connection to these "forgotten" explorers, so kids see that old missions made today's and tomorrow's exploration possible. It is creative because the machines speak for themselves, each with its own personality, and kids experience the engineering rather than just read about it. Dramatized elements are clearly labeled as storytelling, while the facts stay accurate. We built it with HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, using the canvas element for the interactive scenes and the browser SpeechSynthesis API for read-aloud. We used an AI coding assistant to help write the code, and our team checked the facts against NASA data and resources. It runs in any browser with no installation. Along the way we considered accessibility (keyboard navigation, large readable text, high contrast, alt text, read-aloud and reduced-motion support), accuracy, age-appropriate language, and a layout that works on phones and tablets.
